title: Structural signatures of primary and secondary relaxation during physical aging of a metallic glass
authors: Beatrice Baraldi, Stefano Marchesin, Davide Marchesi, Lara Piemontese, Francesco Dallari, Søren S. Sørensen, Eloi Pineda, Marco Di Michiel, Giulio Monaco, Peihao Sun
abstract: Physical aging drives glasses toward equilibrium and changes their thermodynamic and mechanical properties, but the accompanying microscopic structural evolution remains poorly understood. Here, using our recently developed low-background setup combining fast scanning calorimetry with \emph{in-situ} X-ray total scattering, we investigate microscopic structural changes during physical aging in Pd$_{42.5}$Cu$_{30}$Ni$_{7.5}$P$_{20}$ metallic glass. The measurements span an unprecedented six orders of magnitude in time and a temperature range extending from above the glass transition temperature to more than 150\,K below it. We observe dominant structural changes near the first and second peaks of the structure factor. Near and above the glass transition temperature, changes in the first sharp diffraction peak closely follow enthalpy relaxation and are associated predominantly with increasing degrees of medium-range ordering. At lower temperatures, the enthalpy evolution can no longer be described by this contribution alone, revealing an additional, faster relaxation process that correlates with changes near the second diffraction peak and thus short-range structural rearrangements, including increased Pd--Pd correlations. These results establish a direct connection between thermodynamic relaxation and structural evolution, providing strong evidence that primary and secondary aging processes are associated with distinct structural length scales.
summary: This experimental study investigates physical aging in a metallic glass using combined X-ray scattering and calorimetry. By analyzing structural changes associated with the first ($S_1$) and second ($S_2$) diffraction peaks, the authors successfully decouple the total relaxation into two distinct processes. This provides strong evidence that primary aging relates to medium-range ordering, while secondary aging is governed by shorter-range structural rearrangements.
main_problem: The study aims to understand the microscopic structural evolution that occurs during the physical aging process in metallic glasses, specifically distinguishing between primary and secondary relaxation mechanisms.
main_result: The research establishes a direct link between thermodynamic relaxation and structural changes, demonstrating that primary and secondary aging processes are associated with distinct structural length scales (Medium-Range vs. Short-Range Ordering).
method: The authors employed a combination of fast scanning calorimetry (FSC) and in-situ X-ray total scattering to measure structural changes and enthalpy relaxation over vast time and temperature ranges.
model_or_system: The physical system is a metallic glass ($	ext{Pd}_{42.5}	ext{Cu}_{30}	ext{Ni}_{7.5}	ext{P}_{20}$). The analysis models the total enthalpy change as a sum of contributions from primary relaxation (linked to $S_1$) and a secondary relaxation (linked to $S_2$).
key_observables: Structure factor $S(Q)$, Pair Distribution Function (PDF) changes ($\Delta G(r)$), and enthalpy relaxation $\Delta H(t)$ fitted using the Kohlrausch–Williams–Watts (KWW) function.
important_parameters: Temperature range spanning above $T_g$ to $>150 	ext{ K}$ below it; relaxation processes characterized by distinct activation energies ($\sim 336 	ext{ kJ/mol}$ for primary, $\sim 119 	ext{ kJ/mol}$ for secondary).
main_assumptions: The change in PDF ($\Delta G(r)$) is assumed to be proportional to the change in the intensity profile ($\Delta I(Q)$) in the small variation limit.
figures_summary: Figures show the evolution of $S(Q)$ and $\Delta G(r)$ during aging, and plot the relationship between the structural signatures $\delta S_1$ and $\delta S_2$ across different aging temperatures.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the temperature dependence of relaxation kinetics using KWW fitting, first establishing the primary relaxation pathway at higher temperatures, and then introducing a secondary, distinct relaxation pathway at lower temperatures, linking each to a specific structural length scale.
why_interesting: The clear separation of relaxation into distinct structural length scales (MRO vs. SRO) provides a quantitative structural framework for understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in disordered materials, which is relevant to understanding complex energy landscapes in many-body quantum systems.
